newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Market seen under pressure.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Market seen under pressure.

text.p: U.S. credit markets are expected to stay under pressure on Tuesday if the release of fresh housing data confirm forecasts of a substantial rise in construction activity in February, analysts said.

"Tomorrow morning, you're likely to get very strong housing starts numbers ... and the (money) market is not tolerating strong economic data right now," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
In a Reuters survey, Wall Street economists see housing starts rising to 1.45 million units in February against the 1.35 million registered in the previous month.
The data are set for release at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
Analysts said the market has been trying to discount the underlying strength on the U.S. economy as shown by a recent batch of economic indicators.
Lingering fears of a possible rate hike by the Federal Reserve later this month as a "preemptive" strike against inflation are also expected to put a lid on prices on Tuesday.

"The market is concerned about rapid growth and the possibility of a Fed hike in March," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank. "Although he haven't seen inflation yet, people are talking a lot about the Fed being pre-emptive."
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan said recently that he could not rule out the possibility of a Fed hike as a preemptive measure to ward off inflation.
San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank President Robert Parry said on Monday that it is "absolutely essential" for the Fed to be forward looking in its fight against inflation.

The Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee will meet next on March 25. The Fed last changed interest rate levels in January 1996, when it trimmed the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.25 percent.

Credit markets started the week off on the wrong foot, with benchmark 30-year Treasury bond prices falling sharply, boosting the yield to 7.0 percent in the afternoon session, the highest since the close of business on September 23.
The higher yield attracted bargain hunters, who jumped into the market buying securities and bringing the yield back down to 6.96 percent in late trade.

"The market is trying to discount how strong the economy is and the likelihood of a Fed rate hike. Players are pushing the yields up until they can find some buyers," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.
Analysts said there is strong technical resistance around the 7.0 percent level for the 30-year bond yield.
"I personally think 7.0 percent is not too bad. From a technical point of view I'm a buyer at 7.0 percent," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
The Fed added temporary reserves to the market on Monday through overnight system repurchase agreements.
The central bank poured $4.440 billion into the banking system on Monday when fed funds were trading at 5-3/8 percent. The federal funds rate is seen opening at 5.25 percent on Tuesday.
